commandReceipts.command: ls -a; ls kvstore kvstore-cli; cat Cargo.toml 2>/dev/null

notes: The overview reports no cycles and no orphan modules, so the caution section draws instead on disagreements between the source and the two documents in docs/.
docs/adr/adr-0001-layering.md is dated 2026-01-15 and marked Accepted; this explanation describes only what the code at this revision does, not why the two differ.

claims.text: The stated purpose is "a small bounded key-value store with an in-memory cache in front of a file-backed store, driven by a line protocol over the wire" — the same sentence appears as the crate-level doc comment on the library root.
The wire protocol is a colon-separated string: `handle_request` splits on `:`, recognises the verbs `get` and `put`, and answers with `Response::Ok`, `Response::Stored` or `Response::Error`.
Persistence is a directory of files: `FileStore::new` creates a root directory, and `read`/`write` join the key onto that root and hit the filesystem directly.

It is a workspace of exactly two members, `kvstore` and `kvstore-cli`, and neither declares a third-party dependency — the library's `[dependencies]` section is empty and the CLI's only entry is a path dependency on the library, so everything here is std.

Requirements are numbered and testable in the spec — bounded memory with minimal eviction, untrusted input that must never terminate the process, keys confined to the store root, and counters that stay correct under concurrency — which makes SPEC.md the checklist to read each module against.
The library crate holds all four of the workspace's non-trivial modules; the CLI crate is a single file whose whole job is to construct a cache and loop over arguments.
lib.rs is purely a façade: it declares the three modules and re-exports four names — `handle_request`, `Response`, `Cache` and `FileStore` — which is the entire public vocabulary a consumer sees.

The levels in the overview reflect real import direction: cache.rs sits at the bottom because it imports nothing from the crate, api.rs is above it because it imports `crate::cache::Cache`, and storage.rs is above api.rs because it imports `crate::api::Response`.
cache.rs and storage.rs never reference each other, so the in-memory path and the on-disk path can be read, and changed, entirely independently.
The docs directory is part of the structure, not decoration: docs/SPEC.md carries the requirements and docs/adr/adr-0001-layering.md records an accepted decision about which module may import which.

Start with kvstore-cli/src/main.rs: in twelve lines it shows the complete round trip — build a `Cache` with capacity 64, take each command-line argument as a request, hand it to `handle_request`, print the `Response`.
Read api.rs second, because it is where a request becomes a decision: the verb dispatch and the three `Response` variants define what the rest of the system can ever say.
Then cache.rs, which depends on nothing inside the crate and so can be read cold — `new`, `put`, `get` and `evict_oldest` are the whole storage-of-record for anything the CLI does.
Read docs/SPEC.md and docs/adr/adr-0001-layering.md alongside the source rather than after it; both make claims about the code that you can check as you go.
cache.rs is the load-bearing module: three modules depend on it and it depends on none, so its behaviour is felt everywhere and it can be changed without reading anything else in the crate first.
cache.rs also carries most of the crate's public surface — thirteen of its fourteen symbols are public — so almost anything in that file is part of the contract, not an internal detail.

The `Response` enum is the other shared thing: it is both the API's return type and the vocabulary storage.rs uses to report an outcome via `status_response`, so adding or renaming a variant touches both layers.

`Cache` is passed by mutable reference through the whole request path — `handle_request` takes `&mut Cache` and the CLI holds the single owning binding — so there is one cache instance per process and no locking around it.

The layering ADR and the code disagree about direction. ADR-0001 states that `cache` may use `storage` and that `storage` depends on nothing inside the crate, calling upward imports such as `storage` importing `api` prohibited — but storage.rs opens with `use crate::api::Response;` and cache.rs imports nothing from the crate at all.
Despite that inverted edge there are no dependency cycles, because the chain runs storage → api → cache and stops: cache.rs has no outgoing edges.

The "cache in front of a file-backed store" described in the docs is not wired together in the request path: `handle_request` only ever touches `Cache`, and nothing outside lib.rs's re-export references `FileStore`, so a `put` writes to memory and never to disk.

A `put` request is parsed with three chained `unwrap`s — missing key, missing ttl, or a non-numeric ttl each panic — while the doc comment directly above says wire requests are untrusted and SPEC requirement 2 says a malformed request must never terminate the process. `get` by contrast returns an error response.
`evict_oldest` does not evict what its name and doc comment say: documented as evicting the `n` oldest entries, its loop is `for _ in 0..=n`, which runs n+1 times.

`put` also unconditionally pushes to `order` and inserts into `map` without checking whether the key is already present, so re-putting an existing key leaves duplicate entries in the eviction queue while `map.len()` stays the same — the two structures that `put` uses to decide when to evict can drift apart.

`SharedCounter` lives in cache.rs but is not a cache and is not re-exported by lib.rs; its `read_or_init` takes the mutex three separate times in one call, so the check and the insert are not a single critical section — read it against SPEC requirement 4 on concurrent counters.

storage.rs joins the untrusted key straight onto the root path with no rejection of keys that escape it, though the doc comment on `read` notes keys arrive from the wire untrusted and SPEC requirement 3 asks for confinement to the store root.

There is one `unsafe` block in the whole workspace, in `FileStore::magic`, reading a `u32` out of a caller-supplied byte slice via `read_unaligned` after a length check — surprising in a crate that otherwise uses only safe std.
A `put` never stores the value it was given: it stores the formatted string `ttl=<n>`, so a subsequent `get` returns that literal rather than any user data.
There are no test files anywhere in the workspace — the only Rust sources are the four library modules and the CLI main.

output.summary: kvstore is a two-crate Cargo workspace implementing a small bounded key-value store: a `kvstore` library holding a bounded in-memory cache, a text request-handling API, and a file-backed store, plus a `kvstore-cli` binary that feeds command-line arguments through the API one at a time and prints the responses. Requests arrive as colon-separated strings like `get:key` or `put:key:ttl`, are parsed by `handle_request` in api.rs, and are served from the `Cache` in cache.rs; `FileStore` in storage.rs reads and writes values under a root directory. It has no third-party dependencies, and the intended behaviour is written down in docs/SPEC.md and docs/adr/adr-0001-layering.md — both worth reading before the code, and both worth comparing against it.
